questions.problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3},\,{x}_{4}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{4}}?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2},\,{u}_{3}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$, we need to find a fourth vector $x$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{3}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}+{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}-{x}_{4}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}-{x}_{3}-2{x}_{4}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & -1 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are three pivot columns ($1$st, $2$nd and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{4}$ is a free variable. From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-{x}_{4}$ and ${x}_{3}=-2{x}_{4}$, respectively. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+(-{x}_{4})+(-2{x}_{4})+{x}_{4}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2{x}_{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{4} \\ -{x}_{4} \\ -2{x}_{4} \\ {x}_{4}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{4}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{4}=1,$ we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{4}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1 \\ -2\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{4}}=\frac{2}{1}=2.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\}$, respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+0=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=1+0=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0+1=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=0+0=0\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=0-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ only".

questions.problem:
Consider the orthogonal set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]$ such that

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}-6{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to its row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1 & -6 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{6}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & -\frac{37}{6} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-\frac{37}{6}{x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}6{x}_{1}+{x}_{3}=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}{x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{6}{x}_{3} \\ -\frac{37}{6}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=6$, we obtain the vector 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -37 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, an orthogonal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -6\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ -37 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $\frac{{x}_{1}}{{x}_{2}}=\frac{1}{37}.$

questions.problem:
Which of the following sets are orthonormal?

I. $U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\}$

II. $V=\{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\}$

III. $W=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\end{aligned}]\}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of the given sets as 
$\{{u}_{1},{u}_{2}\},$
$\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\},$ and 
$\{{w}_{1},{w}_{2}\}$, respectively. 

The sets $U,V,$ and $W$ are orthonormal if the following conditions on each set hold:

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1}=1 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1}=1 \\ {v}_{2}\cdot {v}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

- ${w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2}=0\,\text{and}\,\{\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{1}=1 \\ {w}_{2}\cdot {w}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine our sets in turn.

- For the set $U,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{6}{13}-\frac{6}{13}=0 & ✓ \\ {u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{13}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{4}{13}+\frac{9}{13}=1 & ✓ \\ {u}_{2}\cdot {u}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{13}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\end{aligned}]=\frac{9}{13}+\frac{4}{13}=1 & ✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, the set $U$ is orthonormal.

- For the set $V,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{v}_{1}\cdot {v}_{1} & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=4+9=13\ne 1 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $V$ is not an orthonormal set.

- For the set $W,$ notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}{w}_{1}\cdot {w}_{2} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} \\ -\frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{29}} \\ \frac{5}{\sqrt{29}}\end{aligned}]=-\frac{4}{29}-\frac{25}{29}=-1\ne 0 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

So, $W$ is not an orthonormal set.

Therefore, we conclude that the correct answer is "$U$ only".

questions.problem:
Consider the **orthonormal** set $U$ below. By adding a new vector $x=[{x}_{1},\,{x}_{2},\,{x}_{3}]^{T},$ extend the set so that it forms an **orthonormal** basis of ${R}^{3}.$ What is the value of $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|?$

$$
U=\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]\}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote the vectors of $U$ as ${u}_{1},\,{u}_{2}.$ To extend the given set to an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$, we need to find a third vector $x$ such that $‖x‖=1,$ and

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{u}_{1}\cdot x=0 \\ {u}_{2}\cdot x=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{1}-\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{2}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}{x}_{3}=0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{1}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}{x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we consider the augmented matrix $M$ of the system above and reduce it to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} & -\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} & 0 \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0 & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\sqrt{17}\cdot {R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=\sqrt{2}\cdot {R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}-{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns ($1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=\frac{4}{3}{x}_{3},$ and from the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}={x}_{3}.$

So, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ \frac{4}{3}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting ${x}_{3}=3,$ we obtain the vector 
$x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ 

Now, we need to normalize $x.$ Notice that $‖x‖=\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}+{3}^{2}}=\sqrt{34}.$ So, we normalize $x$ as follows:

$$
\frac{x}{‖x‖}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, an orthonormal basis of ${R}^{3}$ is

$$
\{[\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{\sqrt{17}} \\ -\frac{3}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ 0 \\ -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{4}{\sqrt{34}} \\ \frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}\end{aligned}]\}.
$$

Finally, $|{x}_{1}|+|{x}_{2}|+|{x}_{3}|=|\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}|+|\frac{4}{\sqrt{34}}|+|\frac{3}{\sqrt{34}}|=\frac{10}{\sqrt{34}}.$
